learn: A just-right book is one you can read with only a few tricky words on each page.
Try the five-finger test: read a page and put up a finger for each word you don't know. Zero or one finger is too easy. Two or three is just right. Five is too hard for now.
Reading just-right books every day makes you a stronger reader.
check: In the five-finger test, how many fingers means "just right"?
A few tricky words on each page
It makes you a stronger reader
It is a rule for grown-ups
lessons.try: Do the five-finger test on two books from your shelf.

learn: Reading stamina is how long you can read and stay focused.
Find a quiet spot, get comfortable and set a timer for ten or fifteen minutes.
Add a few more minutes each week. Your reading muscles grow like any muscle.
check: How long you can read and stay focused
Add a few more minutes each week
lessons.try: Read for 15 minutes without stopping. Write down the page you reached.

learn: Readers talk about books to understand them better.
You can share your favourite part, a question you have, or a connection to your own life.
A connection might be: "This reminds me of when I lost my dog."
check: Why do readers talk about books?
This reminds me of my trip
What can you share about a book?
lessons.try: Tell someone about a book you read this week and make one connection.

learn: Open a book to any page and read it out loud.
Hold up one finger for every word you don't know.
Zero or one finger is easy. Two or three is just right. Five is too hard for now.
check: Five unknown words on one page means the book is...
Two or three unknown words means the book is...
For the check you hold up a finger for each...
lessons.try: Do the five finger check on a book from the class shelf.

learn: Good readers find a quiet, comfy place to read.
Good light helps your eyes. A spot with no TV helps your brain.
You can read in the library, in bed, on a bus or under a tree.
check: Which is a fine place to read?
In the middle of a road
lessons.try: Draw your best reading spot and tell why it works.

learn: A reading goal is something you want to get better at.
It could be reading longer, reading new kinds of books or reading smoothly.
Write your goal down and check on it every week.
check: A reading goal is something you want to...
lessons.try: Write one reading goal for this month.

learn: A book log is a list of what you read.
Write the title, the author, the date and how many minutes you read.
Your log shows how much you have grown as a reader.
check: A book log is a list of...
The person who wrote a book is the...
A book log shows how much you have...
lessons.try: Start a book log and fill in today's reading.

learn: Fiction is a made-up story. Nonfiction tells true facts.
A story about a talking bear is fiction. A book about real bears is nonfiction.
Both kinds of books are worth reading.
check: A book of true facts about bears is...
lessons.try: Sort five books into fiction and nonfiction piles.

learn: Fluent readers read smoothly, not word... by... word.
They read at a good speed, like they are talking.
Rereading a page helps you read it more smoothly.
check: Rereading a page helps you read more...
lessons.try: Read a page three times and notice how it gets smoother.

learn: Expression means your voice shows feeling.
A question mark makes your voice go up. An exclamation mark makes it strong.
Change your voice for different characters.
check: A question mark makes your voice go...
An exclamation mark makes your voice...
lessons.try: Read the line "Look out!" in a calm voice, then with expression.

learn: Good readers notice when something doesn't make sense.
Then they stop, go back and reread.
Ask: Does it look right? Does it sound right? Does it make sense?
check: When reading doesn't make sense, you should...
Which is a good check question?
Good readers ___ when something is wrong.
lessons.try: Listen to a partner read and help them fix one mistake kindly.

learn: Readers make pictures in their minds as they read.
Words that tell how things look, sound and smell help.
Your mind movie helps you remember the story.
check: Making pictures in your mind is called...
Which words help you make a mind picture?
lessons.try: Read a paragraph, close your eyes and draw what you saw.

learn: A prediction is a smart guess about what will happen next.
Use clues from the pictures and the words.
Read on to check if you were right. It's fine to be wrong.
check: If your prediction was wrong, that's...
lessons.try: Stop halfway through a story and predict the ending.

learn: To retell, tell the story in your own words, in order.
Use first, next, then and last.
Tell only the important parts.
check: A retell is told in your own...
lessons.try: Retell a fairy tale to a partner using first, next, then, last.

learn: Reading partners take turns reading pages out loud.
The listener follows along and helps kindly.
After reading, partners talk about their favourite part.
check: After reading, partners talk about their...
lessons.try: Read a book with a partner, taking turns each page.

learn: Every vowel can make a short sound or a long sound.
A short vowel is often alone between consonants: hat, pet, sit, hop, cup.
A long vowel says its own name: hate, Pete, site, hope, cute.
check: Which word has a short vowel?
Which word has a long vowel?
lessons.try: Sort these words into short and long vowels: map, cake, fin, bike, rob, robe.

learn: A syllable is a word part with one vowel sound.
A closed syllable ends with a consonant, and the vowel is short: cat, rab-bit.
An open syllable ends with a vowel, and the vowel is long: me, go, ti-ger.
check: In a closed syllable, the vowel is usually...
lessons.try: Clap the syllables in tiger, rabbit and robot. Are they open or closed?

learn: Long vowels can be spelled in different ways.
Long a: cake, rain, play. Long e: me, feet, beach. Long o: home, boat, snow.
If you're not sure how to spell a word, try it more than one way and pick the one that looks right.
check: Which word spells long a with ay?
Which word spells long o with oa?
If you're not sure how to spell a long vowel word, you can...
lessons.try: Write three different words with long a, each spelled a different way.

learn: Short a sounds like the a in cat.
Long a says its name, like in cake, rain and play.
Many long a words use a-e, ai or ay.
check: Which word has a long a?
Which word has a short a?
lessons.try: Sort cards: cat, cake, map, rain, hat, play.

learn: Short e sounds like the e in bed.
Long e says its name, like in see, eat and me.
Long e is often spelled ee, ea or e at the end.
check: Which word has a long e?
Which word has a short e?
lessons.try: Write three short e and three long e words.

learn: Short i sounds like the i in pig.
Long i says its name, like in bike, night and fly.
Long i is often spelled i-e, igh or y.
check: Which word has a long i?
Which word has a short i?
In the word fly, y says...
lessons.try: Read: The kite flew high in the night sky.

learn: Short o sounds like the o in hot.
Long o says its name, like in home, boat and snow.
Long o is often spelled o-e, oa or ow.
check: Which word has a long o?
Which word has a short o?
lessons.try: Find long o words in a poem about snow.

learn: Short u sounds like the u in cup.
Long u says its name, like in cute, use and blue.
Long u is often spelled u-e, ue or ew.
check: Which word has a long u?
Which word has a short u?
lessons.try: Make a list: bug, cube, sun, mule, few.

learn: A silent e at the end of a word makes the vowel say its name.
Cap becomes cape. Kit becomes kite. Hop becomes hope.
The e makes no sound itself.
check: Add a magic e to cap and you get...
The magic e makes the vowel...
lessons.try: Add a magic e: tap, pin, cub, not. Read the new words.

learn: Y can be a vowel.
At the end of a short word, y says long i: my, fly, cry.
At the end of a longer word, y says long e: happy, baby, funny.
check: In my, the y sounds like...
In happy, the y sounds like...
lessons.try: Sort: my, happy, fly, baby, try, funny.

learn: A syllable is a beat in a word. Each syllable has one vowel sound.
Cat has one syllable. Rabbit has two. Butterfly has three.
Clap the beats to count them.
check: How many syllables are in rabbit?
How many syllables are in butterfly?
lessons.try: Clap the syllables in your name.

learn: When two consonants sit between vowels, split between them: rab-bit, nap-kin.
Read each part, then put them together.
This helps you read long words.
lessons.try: Split and read: basket, muffin, sunset, picnic.

learn: Sorting words by vowel sound trains your ears.
Listen to the middle sound, not just the letters.
Some words look alike but sound different.
check: Which word has a short vowel?
Which word has a long vowel?
lessons.try: Sort twenty word cards into short and long vowel piles.

learn: Now use your vowel skills in real stories.
When you meet a new word, look at the vowel pattern first.
Try the short sound, then the long sound, and pick what makes sense.
check: For a new word, look first at the...
If one vowel sound doesn't make sense, try...
In "The goat ate oats," which word has short a?
lessons.try: Read a short story and underline every long vowel word.

learn: Let's review all the short and long vowels.
Short: a, e, i, o, u as in cat, bed, pig, hot, cup.
Long: they say their names, as in cake, tree, kite, boat, cute.
check: Which word has a long vowel?
Which word has a short vowel?
lessons.try: Play vowel bingo with your class.

learn: Some vowel pairs glide from one sound to another.
oi and oy say /oy/ as in coin and boy.
ou and ow say /ow/ as in cloud and cow.
check: What sound does oy make in "boy"?
lessons.try: Read: toy, soil, mouth, crown, point, shout.

learn: When r comes after a vowel, it changes the vowel's sound. This is a bossy r.
ar as in car and star. or as in fork and storm.
er, ir and ur all sound the same: her, bird, turn.
check: Which has the same sound as "bird"?
Why is it called a bossy r?
lessons.try: Read: farm, horn, fern, girl, burn, shark.

learn: oo can say /oo/ as in moon or the short sound in book.
Some words have silent letters: the k in knee, the w in write, the b in lamb.
Silent letters must be remembered, because you cannot hear them.
lessons.try: Read: spoon, foot, knock, wrap, thumb.

learn: oi and oy make the same sound, as in coin and boy.
oi is often in the middle of a word: soil, point.
oy is often at the end: toy, joy.
check: oi is often in the ___ of a word.
Coin and boy share the same...
lessons.try: Write five oi and oy words and circle the team.

learn: ou and ow can say "ow" as in cloud and cow.
ow can also say long o, as in snow.
Try both sounds and pick the real word.
lessons.try: Read: The brown cow sat under a cloud.

learn: aw and au make the sound in saw and haul.
aw is often at the end: paw, draw.
au is often in the middle: sauce, launch.
check: au is often in the ___ of a word.
Saw and haul share the same...
lessons.try: Draw a picture with five aw or au things.

learn: When r follows a, it makes the sound in car and star.
The r bosses the vowel and changes its sound.
This is called an r-controlled vowel.
check: Which word is an ar word?
lessons.try: Find five ar words in the classroom.

learn: or makes the sound in corn, fork and storm.
ore also says or, as in more and store.
Read or words by saying the team together.
lessons.try: Read: The storm hit the store by the corn.

learn: er, ir and ur all make the same sound.
Her, bird, and turn all have it.
You have to learn which spelling each word uses.
check: er, ir and ur all make ___ sound.
lessons.try: Sort: her, bird, turn, fern, girl, hurt.

learn: oo can say the sound in moon and food.
oo can also say the sound in book and foot.
Try both and pick the real word.
check: Moon and food have the ___ sound.
Book has the same oo as...
Which word has the oo of spoon?
lessons.try: Sort: moon, book, food, look, spoon, wood.

learn: Some letters are silent.
In knee and knot, the k is silent. In write and wrap, the w is silent.
In gnat and sign, the g is silent.
check: In knee, the silent letter is...
In write, the silent letter is...
In gnat, the silent letter is...
lessons.try: Write knee, write and gnat and cross out the silent letter.

learn: In lamb and thumb, the b is silent.
In walk and talk, the l is silent.
Silent letters were said long ago but we stopped saying them.
check: In lamb, the silent letter is...
In talk, the silent letter is...
lessons.try: Read: The lamb can walk and talk.

learn: c says s before e, i or y: city, cent, cycle.
g says j before e, i or y: gem, giant, gym.
Otherwise c says k and g says g: cat, go.
lessons.try: Sort: cat, city, go, gem, cup, giant.

learn: Let's review vowel teams and tricky sounds.
Team sounds: oi/oy, ou/ow, aw/au, oo. Bossy r: ar, or, er, ir, ur.
Silent letters and soft c and g also trick readers.
check: Which word has a bossy r?
Which word has a silent letter?
lessons.try: Make a poster of tricky sounds with one example each.

learn: Hunt for tricky sounds in real books.
Write each word you find under the right sound.
Check with a partner.
check: Where do you hunt for tricky sounds?
Write each word under the right...
lessons.try: Find ten tricky-sound words in your library book.

learn: Main characters are the most important people or animals in the story.
We learn about characters from what they say, do, think and feel.
Characters can change by the end of the story.
check: How do we learn about characters?
What they say, do, think and feel
The most important person in the story
lessons.try: Pick a character from a book and list three words that describe them.

learn: The setting is where and when the story happens.
Settings can be real places, like a city, or make-believe places, like a castle in the clouds.
Authors use describing words so you can picture the setting.
check: Where and when the story happens
Authors help you picture the setting with...
lessons.try: Draw the setting of your favourite story.

learn: The plot is what happens in the story.
Most plots have a problem that the characters try to solve.
In "The Three Little Pigs", the problem is the wolf. The solution is the brick house.
check: In "The Three Little Pigs", what is the problem?
What solves the problem in that story?
lessons.try: Name the problem and solution in a story you know.

learn: The main character is the story's most important person or animal.
Minor characters help the story but appear less.
The story is mostly about the main character.
check: The story is mostly about the...
In Goldilocks, the main character is...
lessons.try: Name the main and minor characters in Goldilocks.

learn: A trait is what a character is like inside: brave, kind, greedy, shy.
We learn traits from what characters say and do.
Use evidence: "She is brave because she..."
check: A trait tells what a character is like...
We learn traits from what characters...
lessons.try: Pick a character and write two traits with evidence.

learn: Characters often change from the start to the end of a story.
A selfish character might learn to share.
Ask: How is the character different at the end?
check: Characters often change from the ___ to the end.
A selfish character might learn to...
Ask how the character is ___ at the end.
lessons.try: Draw a character at the start and at the end.

learn: Setting is where and when the story happens.
Place could be a forest, city or ship. Time could be night, winter or long ago.
Clue words like "once upon a time" tell time.
check: Setting is where and ___ a story happens.
lessons.try: Find the setting words in the first page of a story.

learn: The setting can make a story spooky, happy or exciting.
A storm can cause problems for characters.
If the setting changed, the story would change too.
check: If the setting changed, the story would...
lessons.try: Retell Little Red Riding Hood set in a city.

learn: Every story has a beginning, a middle and an end.
The beginning meets characters. The middle has the problem. The end solves it.
Use these parts to understand any story.
check: The problem usually comes in the...
We meet the characters in the...
The problem is solved at the...
lessons.try: Fold paper in three and draw the beginning, middle and end of a story.

learn: The problem is what goes wrong. The solution is how it gets fixed.
In The Three Little Pigs, the wolf is the problem.
The brick house is the solution.
check: The solution is how the problem gets...
In The Three Little Pigs, the problem is the...
lessons.try: Write the problem and solution of your favourite story.

learn: A story map is a chart that shows the story elements.
It has boxes for characters, setting, problem, events and solution.
Story maps help you remember and retell.
check: A story map shows the story's...
Which belongs in a story map box?
lessons.try: Fill in a story map for The Gingerbread Man.

learn: Events are what happens in the story.
Important events move the story forward.
Put them in order using first, next, then and last.
check: Events are what ___ in a story.
Which word helps put events in order?
lessons.try: List four important events in Jack and the Beanstalk.

learn: Many stories have different versions.
Cinderella stories are told all over the world.
Compare: What is the same? What is different?
check: To compare, ask what is the same and...
lessons.try: Compare two versions of the same fairy tale on a chart.

learn: Pictures also tell about characters and setting.
Faces show feelings. Backgrounds show the setting.
Good readers use words and pictures together.
check: Good readers use words and ___ together.
lessons.try: Cover the words and tell a story only from pictures.

learn: Characters are who. Setting is where and when.
Plot is what happens: problem, events and solution.
Every story you read has these elements.
lessons.try: Teach a younger child the story elements.

learn: A fable is a short story, often with animals, that teaches a lesson called a moral.
In Aesop's "The Ant and the Grasshopper", the ant works all summer while the grasshopper plays. In winter, the ant has food.
The moral is: work hard now and be ready for later.
check: A short story that teaches a lesson
lessons.try: Retell "The Ant and the Grasshopper" and say its moral.

learn: Characters have feelings, just like real people.
Look for clue words like smiled, cried, stomped or trembled.
Their feelings can change when things happen.
lessons.try: Find three feeling clues in a story.

learn: Different characters can see the same event in different ways.
In "Goldilocks and the Three Bears", Goldilocks thinks she found a nice house. The bears think someone broke into their home.
Try reading a part aloud in a different voice for each character.
check: Do characters always see things the same way?
How did the bears feel about Goldilocks?
How can you show different characters when reading aloud?
Use a different voice for each
lessons.try: Retell Goldilocks from Baby Bear's point of view.

learn: A moral is the lesson a story teaches.
Fables often say their moral at the end.
"Slow and steady wins the race" is a moral.
check: A moral is the ___ a story teaches.
Fables often say the moral at the...
"Slow and steady wins the race" is from...
lessons.try: Read The Tortoise and the Hare and say the moral.

learn: The ant works all summer storing food. The grasshopper plays.
In winter, the grasshopper is hungry.
The moral: work today to be ready for tomorrow.
lessons.try: Act out the fable with a partner.

learn: A lion lets a tiny mouse go.
Later the mouse frees the lion from a net.
The moral: little friends can be great friends.
check: The lion was caught in a...
The moral: little friends can be...
lessons.try: Draw the mouse helping the lion.

learn: A shepherd boy lies about a wolf for fun.
When a real wolf comes, nobody believes him.
The moral: liars are not believed even when they tell the truth.
check: When the real wolf came, people...
lessons.try: Talk about why telling the truth matters.

learn: Folktales were told out loud for many years before being written.
Every country has its own folktales.
They often teach how to be wise, kind or clever.
check: Folktales often teach how to be...
lessons.try: Listen to a folktale from another country and share its lesson.

learn: In trickster tales, a clever character tricks others.
Anansi the spider and Br'er Rabbit are tricksters.
Sometimes the trickster gets tricked too.
lessons.try: Tell how a trickster solved a problem with brains, not strength.

learn: Feelings words tell how a character feels.
Happy, sad, angry, scared, proud, nervous and excited are feelings words.
Using exact words helps readers understand.
lessons.try: Make a feelings chart with faces and words.

learn: Authors don't always name feelings. They show them.
"Her hands shook" shows she is scared.
"He jumped and cheered" shows he is happy.
check: "He jumped and cheered" shows he feels...
Authors often ___ feelings instead of naming them.
lessons.try: Find three clues that show how a character feels.

learn: Characters do things for reasons.
A hungry character looks for food. A lonely one looks for a friend.
Ask: Why did the character do that?
check: A good question to ask is...
Why did the character do that?
lessons.try: Pick one action in a story and explain why it happened.

learn: Characters can see the same event differently.
The wolf might tell The Three Little Pigs in another way.
Thinking about other views builds understanding.
check: Characters can see the same event...
A story told by the wolf has a different...
lessons.try: Retell a fairy tale from the villain's view.

learn: When you read dialogue, use a voice that fits the character.
A giant might talk deep and slow. A mouse might squeak.
Voices show feelings and personality.
lessons.try: Read a dialogue with a partner using character voices.

learn: Now write your own fable.
Use animal characters, a short problem and a lesson at the end.
Write the moral as the last line.
lessons.try: Write and illustrate a short fable with a moral.

learn: Nonfiction books are made of paragraphs, and each paragraph has a main topic.
Often the first sentence tells you what the paragraph is about.
The other sentences give details.
check: Where is the main topic often found?
What do the other sentences give?
lessons.try: Read a paragraph in a nonfiction book and say its main topic.

learn: Nonfiction uses features to help readers find information.
Bold words are important. A glossary explains them. An index lists topics and their pages.
Diagrams show parts of something, with labels.
check: What lists topics and their pages?
lessons.try: Find the glossary and the index in a nonfiction book.

learn: Good readers ask questions before, during and after reading.
Who, what, where, when, why and how questions help you understand.
Look back in the text to find the answers.
check: Where do you find the answers?
lessons.try: Write two questions about a topic, then read to find the answers.

learn: Nonfiction teaches us true facts about the real world.
People read it to learn, to answer questions and to make things.
You can read nonfiction in any order, using the contents page.
check: Which helps you find a part of a nonfiction book?
lessons.try: Write a question, then find a nonfiction book that answers it.

learn: The contents page lists the chapters and their page numbers.
It is at the front of the book.
Use it to jump straight to what you need.
check: The contents page is at the...
lessons.try: Use a contents page to find the chapter about food.

learn: The index is at the back. It lists topics in ABC order with pages.
The glossary is a small dictionary for the book's hard words.
Both help you find and understand facts.
lessons.try: Look up one word in a glossary and one topic in an index.

learn: Headings tell what each section is about.
Bold words are important words, printed darker.
Bold words are often in the glossary.
check: Headings tell what a ___ is about.
Bold words are often found in the...
lessons.try: Read only the headings of a chapter and guess what you will learn.

learn: Photos show real things. Captions are sentences under photos.
Labels name the parts of a picture.
These features add facts the words might not say.
check: Labels name the ___ of a picture.
lessons.try: Draw an animal and label five parts.

learn: A diagram is a drawing that shows how something works or its parts.
A chart shows information in rows and columns.
Read the title and labels first.
lessons.try: Read a diagram of a plant and name what each part does.

lessons.t: Main Topic of a Whole Book
learn: The main topic is what the whole book is about.
Look at the title, cover and headings.
Each chapter tells part of the main topic.
check: The main topic is what the ___ is about.
To find the topic, look at the...
Each chapter tells ___ of the main topic.
lessons.try: Name the main topic of three nonfiction books.

learn: Key details are facts that tell about the main topic.
If the topic is frogs, a key detail is "Frogs lay eggs in water."
Details that don't fit the topic are not key details.
check: For a book about frogs, which is a key detail?
Details that don't fit the topic are...
lessons.try: Find three key details about the main topic of a page.

learn: Authors write to inform, to persuade or to entertain.
A book about volcanoes informs. A funny story entertains.
An ad that says "Buy this!" persuades.
check: A book about volcanoes is written to...
An ad that says "Buy this!" wants to...
A funny story is written to...
lessons.try: Sort five texts by the author's purpose.

learn: Some nonfiction tells how to do something in steps.
Signal words like first, next, then and finally show the order.
Doing steps out of order can go wrong.
check: Which is a signal word for steps?
Doing steps out of order can...
"How to plant a seed" is a...
lessons.try: Write the steps for brushing your teeth.

lessons.t: Comparing Two Texts on a Topic
learn: Two books about the same topic may give different facts.
Compare: What did both books say? What did only one say?
Using two sources gives you more facts.
check: Two books on one topic may give...
A comparing chart shows what is the same and...
lessons.try: Read two short texts about owls and make a chart.

learn: An expert knows a lot about one topic.
Read many books on one topic to become an expert.
Share what you learned with your class.
check: An expert knows a lot about...
To become an expert, read ___ books on a topic.
lessons.try: Choose a topic and read three books about it this week.

learn: A collective noun names a group: a flock of birds, a herd of cows, a team of players.
Some nouns have irregular plurals: one foot, two feet; one mouse, two mice; one tooth, two teeth.
These must be remembered.
check: A group of birds is a...
lessons.try: Write the plurals of man, goose and child.

learn: Many verbs add ed to show the past: walk, walked.
Irregular verbs change: sit, sat; run, ran; go, went; tell, told.
The verb must match when the action happened.
lessons.try: Write five sentences about yesterday using past tense verbs.

learn: Adjectives describe nouns: a tall tree, a soft blanket.
Adverbs describe verbs, often telling how: she ran quickly, he spoke softly.
Many adverbs end in ly.
lessons.try: Add an adjective and an adverb to: "The dog barked."

learn: A common noun names any person, place or thing: girl, city, dog.
A proper noun names a special one and starts with a capital: Maria, Paris, Rex.
Days, months and holidays are proper nouns too.
lessons.try: Write five common nouns and a proper noun for each.

lessons.t: Plural Nouns with s and es
learn: Plural means more than one.
Add s to most nouns: cats, books.
Add es to nouns ending in s, x, ch or sh: buses, boxes, lunches, dishes.
check: Add es to words ending in...
lessons.try: Make plurals: fox, bell, wish, bench, cup.

learn: Some plurals don't follow the rule.
One child, two children. One man, two men. One foot, two feet.
Some stay the same: one sheep, two sheep. One fish, two fish.
lessons.try: Make an irregular plural memory game.

learn: A pronoun takes the place of a noun.
I, you, he, she, it, we and they are pronouns.
Instead of "Sam ate. Sam laughed," say "Sam ate. He laughed."
check: A pronoun takes the place of a...
"Mia and I" can be replaced by...
lessons.try: Rewrite three sentences using pronouns.

learn: Reflexive pronouns end in self or selves.
Myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, themselves.
"I made it myself" means nobody else helped.
check: Reflexive pronouns end in self or...
lessons.try: Write a sentence about something you did by yourself.

learn: An action verb tells what someone does: run, jump, read, swim.
Every sentence needs a verb.
Strong verbs make writing exciting: dash instead of go.
check: Which is a stronger verb than "go"?
lessons.try: Act out ten verbs while a partner guesses them.

learn: Present tense tells what is happening now: I walk.
Past tense tells what already happened: I walked.
Many past tense verbs end in ed.
check: The past tense of jump is...
Many past tense verbs end in...
lessons.try: Change five verbs from present to past.

learn: Some verbs change in a special way in the past.
Sit becomes sat. Go becomes went. Run becomes ran. See becomes saw.
You have to learn these by heart.
check: The past tense of go is...
The past tense of see is...
The past tense of sit is...
lessons.try: Play a past tense matching game.

learn: Adjectives describe nouns.
They tell what kind, how many or which one: red ball, three cats, that hat.
Adjectives help readers make mind pictures.
lessons.try: Describe an apple using five adjectives.

learn: Add er to compare two: tall, taller.
Add est to compare three or more: tallest.
"The giraffe is the tallest animal."
check: To compare three or more, add...
lessons.try: Compare three classroom objects by size.

learn: Adverbs describe verbs. Many end in ly.
They tell how, when or where: ran quickly, came today, looked outside.
Adverbs make action clearer.
lessons.try: Add an adverb to five sentences.

learn: Nouns name. Verbs act. Adjectives describe nouns. Adverbs describe verbs.
Pronouns take the place of nouns.
Every word in a sentence has a job.
lessons.try: Colour-code a sentence: nouns blue, verbs red, adjectives green.

learn: A complete sentence has a subject (who or what) and a predicate (what they do or are).
"The frog jumped" is complete. "The frog" is not.
Fix incomplete sentences by adding the missing part.
lessons.try: Make "Ran to the park." into a complete sentence.

learn: You can join two short sentences with and, but, or, or so.
"I like apples. I like pears." becomes "I like apples and pears."
"It rained. We stayed inside." becomes "It rained, so we stayed inside."
check: "I like apples and pears" joins two ideas with...
"It rained, so we stayed inside" shows...
lessons.try: Join these: "I was hungry. I ate a snack."

learn: Capitalise names, places, days, months and holidays: Monday, July, Texas.
Use commas in dates (July 4, 1776) and in a greeting of a letter (Dear Sam,).
An apostrophe can join two words (do not becomes don't) or show who owns something (the dog's bone).
check: The bone belongs to the dog
lessons.try: Write today's date with a comma and one sentence with an apostrophe.

learn: The subject is who or what the sentence is about.
The predicate tells what the subject does or is.
"The dog / barked loudly." Subject, then predicate.
check: In "The bird sang," the subject is...
The predicate tells what the subject...
A complete sentence needs a subject and a...
lessons.try: Draw a line between subject and predicate in five sentences.

learn: A statement tells something and ends with a period.
A question asks and ends with a question mark.
A command tells someone to do something. An exclamation shows strong feeling and ends with !
lessons.try: Write one of each kind about recess.

learn: A fragment is a broken sentence missing a part.
"Ran to the park." Who ran? Add a subject: "Lily ran to the park."
Read your sentences to check they are complete.
check: "Ran to the park" is missing a...
lessons.try: Fix five fragments.

learn: A run-on joins too many ideas without stopping.
"I like cats they are soft" is a run-on.
Fix it with a period or a joining word: "I like cats because they are soft."
check: I like cats they are soft
lessons.try: Fix three run-ons two different ways.

lessons.t: Joining With and, but, or, so
learn: Joining words connect two short sentences.
And adds. But shows a difference. Or gives a choice. So shows a result.
"It rained, so we stayed in."
check: Which joining word shows a choice?
Which joining word shows a difference?
lessons.try: Join five pairs of sentences with the right word.

learn: Make sentences more interesting by adding details.
Add who, what, where, when or how.
"The cat slept" becomes "The fluffy cat slept on my bed all morning."
lessons.try: Expand three short sentences.

learn: Capitalise people's names, pet names, cities, states and countries.
Capitalise days, months and holidays.
Capitalise the word I.
lessons.try: Fix the capitals in a postcard.

learn: Use commas to separate three or more things in a list.
"I packed socks, shirts and a hat."
Use a comma after the greeting and closing of a letter: Dear Ana, Love, Ben
check: In a letter, a comma comes after the...
I like red, blue and green.
I, like red blue and green.
I like red blue, and, green.
lessons.try: Write a list sentence of four favourite foods.

learn: A contraction joins two words and drops letters.
An apostrophe shows where the letters were: can not → can't, I am → I'm.
Do not → don't. It is → it's.
lessons.try: Make contractions for: we are, she is, did not.

learn: Add 's to show something belongs to someone.
"The dog's bone" means the bone belongs to the dog.
"Mia's book" means the book belongs to Mia.
lessons.try: Write five sentences showing who owns what.

learn: A dictionary lists words in ABC order with meanings.
Guide words at the top show the first and last word on the page.
Use it to check spelling and meaning.
check: Guide words show the ___ words on a page.
A dictionary helps check spelling and...
lessons.try: Look up three words and write their meanings.

learn: Before you finish, check your sentences.
Capitals? Punctuation at the end? Complete sentences? Spelling?
Use a checklist every time you write.
check: Which is on an editing checklist?
lessons.try: Use the checklist on a piece of your writing.

learn: Before writing, plan your characters, setting and problem.
A story map has boxes for beginning, middle and end.
Planning helps you know where your story is going.
check: What should you plan before writing?
A story map has boxes for...
Know where your story is going
lessons.try: Fill in a story map for a new story.

learn: Details help readers see, hear and feel your story.
Dialogue is what characters say. Put the words they say inside quotation marks: "Help!" yelled Max.
Strong verbs like dashed or whispered are better than plain verbs like went or said.
check: Where do the spoken words go?
lessons.try: Add one line of dialogue and one strong verb to your story.

learn: Revising means making your writing better: adding details, changing words or moving parts.
Editing means fixing capitals, punctuation and spelling.
Read your story aloud. It helps you hear what to fix.
check: What helps you hear what to fix?
lessons.try: Revise one part of your story and edit it for capitals and periods.

learn: Story ideas come from your life, your dreams, books and "what if" questions.
What if a cat could fly? What if you shrank?
Keep an idea list in your notebook.
check: What if a cat could fly?
lessons.try: Write five "what if" story ideas.

learn: Give your main character a name, a look and traits.
What does your character want? What are they afraid of?
A character with wants makes a good story.
check: Traits tell what a character is like...
Which question helps build a character?
lessons.try: Draw your character and write three facts about them.

learn: Decide where and when your story happens.
Use your senses: what can the character see, hear and smell?
Setting details pull readers into the story.
check: "The air smelled like salt" uses the sense of...
lessons.try: Write three sentences about your story's setting using senses.

learn: Plan the beginning, middle and end before writing.
The middle has a problem. The end solves it.
Use a story map or boxes to plan.
lessons.try: Plan your story on a story map.

learn: A strong beginning hooks the reader.
Start with action, a sound, a question or dialogue.
"CRASH! The window broke." is a hook.
check: You can start with action, a sound or...
lessons.try: Write three different beginnings for your story.

learn: Time words show when things happen.
First, next, then, after that, later, finally.
They help readers follow the order.
check: Time words help readers follow the...
Which word often ends a story's events?
lessons.try: Add time words to your story draft.

learn: Show how characters feel instead of just telling.
Not "Sam was scared," but "Sam's knees shook."
Showing makes readers feel it too.
lessons.try: Rewrite three "telling" sentences to "showing" ones.

learn: Dialogue is what characters say.
Put quotation marks around the spoken words: "Let's go!" said Max.
Start a new line when a new person talks.
check: When a new person talks, start a...
lessons.try: Write a short conversation between two characters.

learn: A good ending solves the problem.
It can show how the character feels or what they learned.
Avoid "and then I woke up."
check: An ending can show what the character...
lessons.try: Write two possible endings and choose the best.

learn: Revising means making your writing better.
Add details, change weak words, cut parts that don't fit.
Read your story out loud to hear what to change.
lessons.try: Revise your story by adding five details.

learn: A writing partner reads your story and gives kind ideas.
Use "I liked..." and "Could you add...?"
Listen and decide what to change.
check: After feedback, you ___ what to change.
lessons.try: Swap stories with a partner and give two stars and a wish.

learn: Publishing means making a neat final copy to share.
Add a cover, a title and pictures.
Share your story by reading it aloud to the class.
check: Publishing means making a ___ final copy.
A published story can have a...
lessons.try: Publish your story as a little book.

learn: In opinion writing, state your opinion, give reasons, and end with a conclusion.
Use linking words like because, also and for example.
"Recess should be longer because exercise helps us learn. Also, we can make friends."
check: What comes first in opinion writing?
What do you give to support an opinion?
lessons.try: Write an opinion paragraph about the best season, with two reasons.

learn: A friendly letter has a date, a greeting, a body, a closing and a signature.
The greeting starts with "Dear" and ends with a comma: Dear Grandma,
The closing might be "Love," or "Your friend," followed by your name.
lessons.try: Write a friendly letter to someone in your family.

learn: Research means finding facts about a topic.
Use books, trusted websites or ask an expert, like a librarian.
Take notes in your own words and write down where you found each fact.
lessons.try: Research an animal and write three facts with where you found them.

learn: A fact can be proved true. An opinion is what someone thinks or feels.
"Dogs have four legs" is a fact. "Dogs are the best pets" is an opinion.
Words like best, worst and should often show opinions.
check: "Pizza is the best food" is an...
Which word often shows an opinion?
lessons.try: Sort ten sentences into fact and opinion.

learn: Begin opinion writing by saying what you think.
Use "I think," "I believe" or "In my opinion."
Be clear so readers know where you stand.
check: "In my opinion, recess should be longer" is an...
lessons.try: Write an opinion sentence about the best season.

learn: Support your opinion with reasons.
Use because, also, and another reason is.
Good reasons convince the reader.
lessons.try: Give three reasons for your opinion.

learn: End by saying your opinion again in new words.
"That is why I think..." is a good conclusion.
The ending wraps up your writing.
check: That is why I think cats are great.
lessons.try: Write a conclusion for your opinion piece.

learn: A book review tells your opinion about a book.
Tell the title, a little about it, and whether you recommend it and why.
Don't give away the ending!
check: A book review tells your ___ about a book.
In a review, don't give away the...
A review says if you ___ the book.
lessons.try: Write a review of a book you read this month.

learn: A friendly letter has five parts.
Date, greeting, body, closing and signature.
"Dear Grandma," is a greeting. "Love," is a closing.
check: How many parts does a friendly letter have?
Your name at the end is the...
lessons.try: Label the five parts on a sample letter.

learn: A thank-you letter tells someone you are grateful.
Say what they did and why it mattered to you.
Be specific and kind.
check: A thank-you letter shows you are...
Say what they did and why it...
lessons.try: Write a thank-you letter to someone at school.

learn: The receiver's address goes in the middle.
Your return address goes in the top left corner.
The stamp goes in the top right corner.
check: The stamp goes in the top...
The receiver's address goes in the...
Your return address goes in the top...
lessons.try: Address an envelope to a classmate.

learn: Research starts with a question you want answered.
"What do sharks eat?" is a good research question.
Write questions before you start reading.
lessons.try: Write three questions about an animal.

learn: Look for facts in books, encyclopedias and trusted websites.
Use headings and the index to find answers fast.
Make sure facts come from a reliable source.
check: Use the ___ to find answers fast.
lessons.try: Find two facts that answer one of your questions.

learn: Notes are short words, not whole copied sentences.
Write key words and facts in your own words.
Write where you found each fact.
lessons.try: Take notes on one page of a nonfiction book.

learn: Turn your notes into a short report with a topic sentence and facts.
Add a picture with a caption.
Present it to the class and answer questions.
check: A picture in a report should have a...
lessons.try: Present your research report.
